situation:
You and your partner serve as the seller community manager and the trust and safety manager at THISTLEBOUND MARKET, an online marketplace where independent artisans list and sell handmade goods. The chief executive officer (judge) has asked you to meet before the company answers a settlement offer that arrived this week. Thistlebound has run the marketplace for twelve years and now lists work from roughly forty thousand sellers, most of them one person working out of a home studio.

The company's standing with those sellers rests on a promise printed in its seller agreement and repeated in its marketing: Thistlebound will tell sellers directly and promptly whenever their information is exposed. That promise has been part of how the company holds its ground since OPENLOOM, a lower-fee marketplace launched two years ago, began drawing sellers away, and several of Thistlebound's best-known shops have already moved.

Last spring LARKFIELD ANALYTICS, a reporting vendor Thistlebound has worked with for nine years, misconfigured a server and left seller records readable from outside its systems for several weeks. Those records carried legal names, home shipping addresses, and monthly sales totals. Within a month, a number of Thistlebound's highest-earning sellers were approached at those addresses by recruiters for Openloom, and sellers have been asking the company how their information traveled.

Larkfield has offered to pay Thistlebound enough to fund a full year of fee relief for every affected seller, the same relief the company has not been able to afford while it loses ground on price. The offer carries a nondisclosure term. Thistlebound could tell sellers that an exposure occurred, but could not name Larkfield or explain how the records got out, which is the question the sellers are actually asking.

State notification law requires Thistlebound to tell affected sellers that an exposure happened, and does not require the company to name the vendor, so the term is lawful. Refusing it would leave the company free to give sellers the whole account, but the payment goes with it, the fee relief would have to come out of reserves the company does not have, and Larkfield has signaled it would litigate for years rather than settle in the open.

The chief executive officer (judge) wants your team's recommendation on how Thistlebound should answer Larkfield and how the company should speak to its sellers either way, including what the staff who handle seller support should be able to say. When you enter the office, the chief executive officer (judge) will greet you and ask to hear your ideas. After your presentation and the judge's questions, the judge will thank you for your time.
